query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily controlled by the Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG_BCC-FCC) between the BCC and FCC phases. When the alloy is in the high‐temperature BCC state, a sufficiently large ΔG_BCC-FCC favors the stabilization of the BCC phase; however, if thermal processing (e.g., slower cooling or lower annealing temperatures) reduces this free-energy gap below a critical threshold, the kinetics allow nucleation of an FCC phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy initially processed into a high-temperature BCC phase
generation.intervention: Varying the thermal history through controlled annealing and cooling rates (or slight compositional adjustments near 7% Al) to systematically modify the ΔG_BCC-FCC
generation.conditions: Experiments carried out in an inert atmosphere with well-controlled thermal treatments that avoid oxidation and extraneous kinetic effects, within the temperature regime relevant to BCC stability
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving volume fractions of the BCC and FCC phases during cooling act as the mediator of the overall microstructure
generation.mechanism: A high ΔG_BCC-FCC stabilizes the BCC phase by providing a strong thermodynamic driving force that suppresses nucleation of the FCC phase despite the presence of kinetic factors such as sluggish diffusion. Altering the thermal schedule adjusts ΔG values, and when it falls below a critical value, the FCC phase begins to emerge, indicating that thermodynamic instability—not solely kinetics—governs the phase transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with thermal treatments designed to maintain a high ΔG_BCC-FCC will retain mostly a BCC structure; in contrast, treatments that allow ΔG_BCC-FCC to decrease (e.g., slower cooling or lower annealing temperatures) will show an increasing fraction of FCC formation, with the transformation rate following the thermodynamically predicted trend.
generation.baseline: High-temperature rapid-quenched samples that preserve a large ΔG_BCC-FCC and remain predominantly BCC
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable near the Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 composition within conventional processing windows; it may not hold if extraneous phases form due to oxidation, non-equilibrium processing, or if kinetic barriers become dominant under extreme cooling conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative threshold of ΔG_BCC-FCC needed to trigger the transition is not precisely known, and minor kinetic effects under different cooling regimes may affect the transformation rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy samples and subject them to a series of controlled annealing treatments at different temperatures and cooling rates designed to vary the computed ΔG_BCC-FCC. Use thermodynamic calculations (e.g., via CALPHAD) to estimate ΔG_BCC-FCC for each treatment condition.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification (using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy)
Correlation of phase fractions with thermal history
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples processed under conditions predicted to maintain a high ΔG_BCC-FCC (i.e., conditions expected to suppress FCC nucleation) nonetheless show significant FCC formation, or if there is no systematic correlation between the calculated ΔG_BCC-FCC and the observed phase fractions, then the hypothesis that ΔG_BCC-FCC governs phase stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To generate the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation, we adopt the following strategies: (1) to obtain a single fcc phase in the as-annealed state and (2) to increase the thermal stability of bcc phase at low temperature. It is well known that a key parameter for designing metastable MEAs as well as conventional structural alloys which show the TRIP behavior, i.e., the fcc to bcc transformation, is the stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc. Though the SFE contains a term expressed by a difference in Gibbs free energies between hcp and fcc phases,,, the fcc to bcc transformation is also analyzed by the SFE. In this study, however, we reveal that a difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases can be a critical parameter for the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation. The phase equilibrium and stability were calculated by using a Thermo-Calc software along with the thermodynamic database TCFE2000 and its upgraded version. This CALPHAD approach is much more effective than trial-and-error-based conventional alloy-design approaches consuming a lot of costs and time,. The above results reveal that our design approach based on the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc) can realize the fcc to bcc transformation in MEA research areas. The fraction of bcc and consequent transformation rate according to the Co content and temperature also well correspond to the thermodynamic phase stability.
